cues.text: Integration reverses differentiation when we seek an antiderivative.
Call the integrand lowercase f and a candidate antiderivative capital F.
If differentiating capital F gives lowercase f throughout an interval, then
capital F is an antiderivative there.
For the integrand two x, one antiderivative is x squared.
Adding any constant leaves its derivative unchanged, so the indefinite
integral
is x squared plus C.
The integral sign with no bounds represents a family of functions, rather than
one number.
The symbol d x identifies the variable of integration.
A different variable is held constant unless dependence is explicitly stated.
On a connected interval, any two antiderivatives of the same function differ
by
a constant.
Separate domain intervals can have independent constants.
For example, one over x excludes zero, so a formula on positive inputs need
not
share its integration constant with a formula on negative inputs.
Linearity lets us integrate sums term by term and pull out constant factors.
It does not turn an integral of a product into a product of integrals.
Differentiate the proposed result and compare it with the entire original
integrand, and check that the original domain restrictions still hold.
The power integration rule increases the exponent by one and divides by that
new exponent.
It applies when the exponent is not negative one, on an interval where the
real
power is defined and differentiable.
Integrating three x squared minus four gives x cubed minus four x plus C.
The exceptional exponent negative one has a logarithmic answer.
An antiderivative of one over x is natural log of absolute x on either
interval
excluding zero.
The absolute value makes a real formula available for negative inputs as well
as positive inputs.
It does not include zero.
The exponential e to the x integrates to itself.
For e to the two x, divide by the inner derivative two, giving one half e to
the two x plus C.
A positive base a different from one gives an integral of a to the x equal to
a
to the x divided by natural log a.
If the base is one, integrate the constant one directly.
Verify the coefficient by differentiating, especially when an exponent
contains
a scale factor.
Trigonometric integration begins by reversing the derivative table, using
radians.
Cosine x integrates to sine x, and sine x integrates to negative cosine x.
Secant squared x integrates to tangent x.
Cosecant squared x integrates to negative cotangent x.
Secant x times tangent x integrates to secant x, while cosecant x times
cotangent x integrates to negative cosecant x.
Check the negative signs by differentiating the proposed answers.
Each formula is used on an interval avoiding the poles of the original
integrand.
A scaled angle changes the coefficient: cosine of three x integrates to sine
of
three x divided by three.
Integrating tangent x gives negative natural log of absolute cosine x plus C.
This follows by substituting cosine x and using its derivative negative sine
x.
Similarly, cotangent x integrates to natural log of absolute sine x plus C.
The logarithm formulas keep the excluded zeros visible.
No ordinary antiderivative formula permits crossing a pole as though the
function were continuous there.
Identify the integrand as a complete pattern before selecting a table entry.
Substitution reverses the chain rule.
Look for an inner expression together with a constant multiple of its
derivative.
In the integral of two x times cosine of x squared, set u equal to x squared.
Then d u equals two x d x, so the whole integral becomes the integral of
cosine
u with respect to u.
The result is sine u plus C, or sine of x squared plus C after returning to x.
Writing a substitution without replacing every remaining x is incomplete.
Another example integrates x times the square root of one plus x squared.
Set u equal to one plus x squared.
Then x d x equals one half d u.
Integrating one half u to the one half gives one third u to the three halves,
hence one third of the quantity one plus x squared raised to three halves,
plus
C.
The derivative check restores the original x factor.
Avoid treating d u as though it always equals d x.
Account for the scale factor before integrating the transformed expression.
The product rule yields integration by parts.
Starting with the differential of u v equal to u d v plus v d u, rearrangement
gives the integral of u d v equal to u v minus the integral of v d u.
Choose the factors so that differentiating u and integrating d v make the
remaining integral manageable.
For x times e to the x, choose u equal to x and d v equal to e to the x d
x.
Then d u is d x and v is e to the x.
The answer is x e to the x minus e to the x plus C.
Differentiation shows the extra exponential terms cancel.
For natural log x on its positive domain, write the hidden product with one,
choose u equal to natural log x and d v equal to d x.
This gives x natural log x minus x plus C.
A factor selection mnemonic is only a guide, not a theorem that every choice
simplifies the problem.
Check signs and boundary terms carefully when applying the same method to a
definite integral.
A rational integrand is a quotient of polynomials.
If the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree, polynomial
division
should come before partial fractions.
For one divided by x times x plus one, write A over x plus B over x plus one.
Multiplying by the common denominator gives one equal to A times x plus one,
plus B x.
Comparing coefficients gives A equal to one and B equal to negative one.
Integration now gives natural log of absolute x minus natural log of absolute
x
plus one, plus C.
The intervals exclude zero and negative one.
Repeated linear factors require a separate term for every power up to the
repeated multiplicity.
An irreducible quadratic factor uses a linear numerator.
For example, a term over x squared plus one should allow numerator A x plus B,
rather than assuming a constant before checking the identity.
Determine the coefficients algebraically, then integrate the simpler pieces.
Differentiating the final logarithmic expression checks both the decomposition
and the integration.
A cancellation in an intermediate expression never authorizes an input
excluded
by the original integrand.
Completing the square reduces a general quadratic to a shifted square plus or
minus a constant.
For x squared plus two x plus five, the result is the square of x plus one,
plus four.
Substituting t equal to x plus one gives the standard integral of one over t
squared plus two squared.
The answer is one half arctangent of the quantity x plus one divided by two,
plus C.
The denominator is positive for every real x.
In general, one over x squared plus a squared integrates to arctangent of x
over a, divided by a, with a positive.
A difference of squares instead gives logarithms.
One over a squared minus x squared integrates to one over two a times natural
log of the absolute value of the ratio a plus x to a minus x.
Reversing the denominator sign reverses the antiderivative sign.
The poles at positive and negative a remain excluded.
Complete the square before choosing between an inverse tangent pattern and a
logarithmic pattern, since the sign of the remaining constant determines the
relevant case.
A linear numerator over a quadratic often contains part of the derivative of
its denominator.
Let Q equal x squared plus two x plus five.
Its derivative is two x plus two.
For numerator two x plus three, write it as Q prime plus one.
The integral separates into Q prime over Q and one over Q.
The first piece is natural log Q because this Q is always positive.
The second piece is the completed square inverse tangent from the previous
chapter.
The answer is natural log of x squared plus two x plus five, plus one half
arctangent of the quantity x plus one divided by two, plus C.
For a general numerator p x plus q, solve the identity p x plus q equal to A Q
prime plus B before integrating.
If the denominator is a square root of Q, the Q prime portion instead
integrates to twice A square root of Q.
The remaining constant portion uses a standard reciprocal square root integral
after completing the square.
Keep a real interval with Q positive when that square root occurs in the
denominator.
Reciprocal square root integrals have different answers depending on the signs
inside the radical.
With a positive, one divided by square root of a squared minus x squared
integrates to arcsine of x over a.
Its ordinary integrand domain is absolute x less than a.
One divided by square root of x squared plus a squared has a logarithmic
antiderivative: natural log of the absolute value of x plus that square root.
The same logarithmic form works for square root of x squared minus a squared
in
the denominator, on either interval where absolute x is greater than a.
Differentiate on the chosen interval to check the sign and domain.
A numerator proportional to the inner derivative is simpler.
The integral of x divided by square root of x squared plus four is just square
root of x squared plus four, plus C.
A linear numerator can be split into a multiple of the quadratic derivative
and
a constant remainder.
After completing the square, the remainder matches one of these reciprocal
radical families.
Endpoint values of an inverse function do not imply the reciprocal radical
integrand is defined at those endpoints.
A square root in the numerator may need a trigonometric substitution rather
than a direct inverse function formula.
For square root of a squared minus x squared, set x equal to a sine theta on a
range where cosine theta is positive.
Then the square root is a cosine theta, d x is a cosine theta d theta, and the
integral becomes a squared times the integral of cosine squared theta.
A half angle identity integrates that expression.
Returning to x gives one half of x times square root of a squared minus x
squared, plus a squared arcsine of x over a.
The inverse branch is chosen consistently with the substitution.
For square root of x squared plus a squared, the answer is one half of x times
the radical plus a squared natural log of the absolute value of x plus the
radical.
For square root of x squared minus a squared, replace that plus logarithmic
term by a minus logarithmic term.
These formulas hold on the appropriate open real intervals.
Verify by differentiation instead of assuming that the signs of the two
logarithmic terms are interchangeable.
A trigonometric integrand may not match the derivative table until an identity
changes its form.
The integral of sine squared x is not sine cubed x divided by three, because
the power rule alone ignores the derivative of sine x.
Instead use sine squared x equal to one half of one minus cosine two x.
Integration gives x over two minus sine two x over four, plus C.
Cosine squared x gives x over two plus sine two x over four, plus C.
Differentiating the oscillating term introduces a factor two, which explains
the denominator four.
The product sine x cosine x can be handled by substitution u equal to sine x,
giving one half sine squared x plus C.
Product to sum identities offer another route and produce an equivalent
antiderivative up to a constant.
For higher powers, preserve a suitable sine or cosine factor when its
differential is useful, and transform the remaining even powers.
Do not multiply separate antiderivatives.
An identity rewrites the integrand.
In substitution, change both the expression and the differential together.
A definite integral describes signed accumulation over an interval.
For a continuous function, divide the interval into small subintervals,
multiply a sampled function value by each width, and take the limit of the sum
as the largest width tends to zero.
For x squared from zero to one, use n equal pieces of width one over n and
right endpoints k over n.
The resulting sum is one over n cubed times the sum of k squared from one
through n.
Using the sum of squares formula, this is n times n plus one times two n plus
one, divided by six n cubed.
Its limit is one third.
This calculation defines the integral without assuming an antiderivative
evaluation first.
For a continuous nonnegative function, this accumulation is area under the
curve.
Negative values contribute negative accumulation, so a definite integral need
not equal total geometric area.
A finite rectangle sum is an approximation, while the limit is the integral.
The integration variable is a dummy variable: replacing x by t consistently
leaves the value of a definite integral unchanged.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects accumulation with
differentiation.
If f is continuous on an interval, the function formed by integrating f from a
fixed starting point to x has derivative f of x.
Write capital F for an antiderivative of lowercase f on the whole integration
interval.
The definite integral from a to b equals capital F evaluated at b, minus
capital F evaluated at a.
For three x squared from zero to two, use x cubed, obtaining eight minus zero,
or eight.
The integration constant cancels in the endpoint subtraction, so no arbitrary
plus C belongs in the final numerical answer.
A variable upper limit needs the chain rule.
Differentiating the integral of cosine t from zero to x squared gives cosine
of
x squared times two x.
A variable lower limit introduces a minus sign.
With both limits variable, differentiate the upper endpoint contribution and
subtract the lower endpoint contribution.
These statements require the relevant continuity conditions.
They do not license endpoint substitution across an interior pole.
Establish that the original integrand is integrable on the full interval
before
applying the ordinary endpoint evaluation rule.
Definite integrals satisfy linearity and interval additivity when the
functions
are integrable on the stated intervals.
Reversing the limits changes the sign, and equal limits give zero.
Splitting at a point c lets the integral from a to b equal the sum from a to c
and c to b.
For a less than b and a nonnegative function, the integral is nonnegative.
If one function stays above another throughout the interval, its integral is
at
least as large.
These facts help check answers and estimate sizes before calculating an
antiderivative.
For example, one plus x squared lies between one and two on zero through one,
so its integral lies between one and two; direct evaluation gives four thirds.
The interval direction matters in inequalities.
Domain restrictions also matter: one over x squared has an interior pole on
negative one through one.
Substituting endpoints into negative one over x would misleadingly give
negative two, despite a positive integrand.
The ordinary definite integral is not defined there; its improper integral
diverges.
Always inspect the entire interval, not only the two endpoint values.
A substitution in a definite integral changes the variable, the differential
and the bounds together.
For two x times e to the x squared from zero to one, set u equal to x squared.
The differential is d u equal to two x d x.
The old lower bound zero gives u equal to zero, and the old upper bound one
gives u equal to one.
Integrating e to the u on those bounds gives e minus one.
For two x divided by one plus x squared on the same interval, instead choose u
equal to one plus x squared.
The new bounds are one and two.
The result is natural log two.
Leaving the old bounds zero and one on that logarithmic integral would be
incorrect and would even introduce an artificial singularity.
Another valid approach finds an antiderivative in x and then uses the original
x bounds.
Do not mix the two approaches halfway through.
If a substitution reverses endpoint order, the transformed differential and
the
oriented bounds together handle the sign.
Check the transformation on the full interval and keep any original domain
exclusions.
Reflection gives a useful definite integral identity.
Replacing x by a plus b minus t reverses the interval, and the negative
differential restores the original order.
Thus the integral of f of x from a to b equals the integral of f of a plus b
minus x over the same bounds.
On a symmetric interval, an integrable odd function has integral zero, while
an
integrable even function gives twice its integral over the positive half.
Integrability is essential: odd appearance cannot cancel an undefined ordinary
integral across a pole.
As a reflection example, let I be the integral of sine x divided by sine x
plus
cosine x from zero to pi over two.
Reflection interchanges sine and cosine, producing another expression for I
with cosine in the numerator and the same denominator.
Adding the two expressions gives two I equal to the interval length pi over
two.
Therefore I equals pi over four.
The denominator stays positive throughout this interval.
Symmetry can remove much of the algebra, but only after checking the interval,
the transformed expression and the denominator conditions.
Geometric area is nonnegative, while a definite integral records sign.
For y equal to x from negative one to one, odd symmetry makes the signed
integral zero.
The two triangular regions have total area one.
To obtain that area by integration, split at zero and integrate negative x on
the negative half, then positive x on the positive half.
For the area between two curves, find their intersection points and decide
which graph is above the other on every part of the interval.
The curves y equal to x and y equal to x squared meet at zero and one.
On the interval between them, x is at least x squared.
The enclosed area is the integral of x minus x squared from zero to one, equal
to one half minus one third, or one sixth.
If the graphs exchange order, split again at the exchange points.
Taking the absolute value of a final signed integral is not generally enough,
because positive and negative pieces may already have cancelled.
A sketch helps establish the correct region and the boundaries before any
antiderivative calculation.
Area integrals also apply to standard curves.
A circle of radius r has upper boundary square root of r squared minus x
squared.
Four times its first quadrant integral from zero to r gives pi r squared,
using
the square root antiderivative or a trigonometric substitution.
For an ellipse x squared over a squared plus y squared over b squared equal to
one, the first quadrant boundary is b times square root of one minus x squared
over a squared.
Substitute x equal to a sine theta.
Four times the resulting quarter area gives pi a b.
The positive parameters a and b are semiaxes, rather than full axis lengths.
A parabola needs additional boundaries to enclose a finite region.
For the upper branch of y squared equal to four a x with a positive, take x
from zero to a and the x axis below.
Integrating two square root of a x gives four a squared over three.
Including the reflected lower region would double that answer.
Always specify the branch and closing lines: naming a curve alone does not
determine a unique finite area.
